claims.claim: The membrane-embedded arm includes a chain of three antiporter-like subunits, NuoL, NuoM, and NuoN.
claims.source: The membrane-embedded arm includes a chain of three antiporter-like subunits, NuoL, NuoM, and NuoN (E. coli nomenclature is used for the subunits hereafter) (Efremov and Sazanov, 2011), which are also found in the Mrp family of multisubunit H+/Na antiporters (Steiner and Sazanov, 2020).
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge about the membrane arm structure, supported by cited references.

claims.claim: The antiporter-like subunits NuoL, NuoM, and NuoN are also found in the Mrp family of multisubunit H+/Na antiporters.
claims.source: The membrane-embedded arm includes a chain of three antiporter-like subunits, NuoL, NuoM, and NuoN (E. coli nomenclature is used for the subunits hereafter) (Efremov and Sazanov, 2011), which are also found in the Mrp family of multisubunit H+/Na antiporters (Steiner and Sazanov, 2020).
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge supported by the cited reference.

claims.claim: Each antiporter-like subunit contains two structural repeats comprising five transmembrane helices (TMH4-8 and TMH9-13).
claims.source: Each antiporter-like subunit contains two structural repeats comprising five transmembrane helices (TMH, TMH4-8, and TMH9-13).
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge about the structure of antiporter-like subunits, supported by prior structural studies.

claims.claim: TMH7 and TMH12 are interrupted by an extended loop in the middle of the membrane.
claims.source: TMH7 and TMH12 are interrupted by an extended loop in the middle of the membrane and the helix TM8 at the interface between symmetric motifs is interrupted by the π-bulge (Baradaran et al., 2013; Efremov and Sazanov, 2011).
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge supported by cited structural studies.

claims.claim: The helix TMH8 at the interface between symmetric motifs is interrupted by the π-bulge.
claims.source: TMH7 and TMH12 are interrupted by an extended loop in the middle of the membrane and the helix TM8 at the interface between symmetric motifs is interrupted by the π-bulge (Baradaran et al., 2013; Efremov and Sazanov, 2011).
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge supported by cited structural studies.

claims.claim: Membrane-embedded NuoH mediates interaction with the peripheral arm.
claims.source: Membrane-embedded NuoH mediates interaction with the peripheral arm and also contains five-helix structural repeat found in antiporter-like subunits (Baradaran et al., 2013).
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge supported by the cited reference.

claims.claim: NuoH contains a five-helix structural repeat found in antiporter-like subunits.
claims.source: Membrane-embedded NuoH mediates interaction with the peripheral arm and also contains five-helix structural repeat found in antiporter-like subunits (Baradaran et al., 2013).
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge supported by the cited reference.

claims.claim: NuoH together with subunits NuoB and NuoD forms an extended ubiquinone-binding cavity (Q-cavity).
claims.source: Together with subunits NuoB and NuoD it forms an extended ubiquinone-binding cavity (Q-cavity) that stretches from the hydrophobic region of the membrane bilayer to the binding site of the ubiquinone head group (Q-site) found in the proximity of the terminal iron-sulfur cluster N2 (Baradaran et al., 2013).
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge supported by the cited reference.

claims.claim: The Q-cavity stretches from the hydrophobic region of the membrane bilayer to the Q-site found in proximity of the terminal iron-sulfur cluster N2.
claims.source: Together with subunits NuoB and NuoD it forms an extended ubiquinone-binding cavity (Q-cavity) that stretches from the hydrophobic region of the membrane bilayer to the binding site of the ubiquinone head group (Q-site) found in the proximity of the terminal iron-sulfur cluster N2 (Baradaran et al., 2013).
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge supported by the cited reference.

claims.claim: The membrane arm features a continuous chain of conserved and functionally important ionizable residues positioned in the middle of the membrane.
claims.source: The membrane arm features a continuous chain of conserved and functionally important ionizable residues positioned in the middle of the membrane. These are suggested to be involved in proton translocation and its coupling to electron transfer (Baradaran et al., 2013; Efremov and Sazanov, 2011).
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge supported by cited references.

claims.claim: The conserved ionizable residues in the membrane arm are suggested to be involved in proton translocation and its coupling to electron transfer.
claims.source: The membrane arm features a continuous chain of conserved and functionally important ionizable residues positioned in the middle of the membrane. These are suggested to be involved in proton translocation and its coupling to electron transfer (Baradaran et al., 2013; Efremov and Sazanov, 2011).
claims.evidence: This is a hypothesis supported by cited references.

claims.claim: Rotation of the cytoplasmic half of TMH3 of NuoJ in mammalian complex I was associated with active-deactive transition.
claims.source: Attempts to visualize conformational changes in the membrane domain (Kampjut and Sazanov, 2020; Parey et al., 2018) have revealed rotation of the cytoplasmic half of TMH3 of NuoJ in mammalian complex I (Agip et al., 2018) and were associated with active-deactive transition.
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge from cited references.

claims.claim: Proton translocation mechanisms without conformational changes in antiporter-like subunits were recently suggested.
claims.source: Recently, proton translocation mechanisms without conformational changes in antiporter-like subunits were suggested (Kampjut and Sazanov, 2020; Steiner and Sazanov, 2020).
claims.evidence: This is based on cited references proposing alternative mechanisms.

claims.claim: All proposed coupling mechanisms remain largely speculative and require further validation.
claims.source: However, all proposed coupling mechanisms remain largely speculative and require further validation by functional, biochemical, and structural methods.
claims.evidence: This is an assessment of the current state of knowledge in the field.

claims.claim: E. coli complex I has been studied using many biophysical and biochemical techniques.
claims.source: It has been studied using many biophysical and biochemical techniques (Verkhovskaya and Bloch, 2013).
claims.evidence: This is supported by the cited reference.

claims.claim: E. coli complex I represents a highly attractive system to study the coupling mechanism due to the possibility of fast and extensive mutagenesis.
claims.source: Combined with the possibility of fast and extensive mutagenesis (Pohl et al., 2007; Verkhovskaya and Bloch, 2013), it represents a highly attractive system to study the coupling mechanism.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the cited capabilities of the E. coli system.

claims.claim: E. coli complex I is fragile and dynamic in nature.
claims.source: However, owing to its fragile and dynamic nature (Verkhovskaya and Bloch, 2013), high-resolution structures of this complex remain limited to a partial structure of the membrane domain (Efremov and Sazanov, 2011).
claims.evidence: This is supported by the cited reference.

claims.claim: High-resolution structures of E. coli complex I were previously limited to a partial structure of the membrane domain.
claims.source: However, owing to its fragile and dynamic nature (Verkhovskaya and Bloch, 2013), high-resolution structures of this complex remain limited to a partial structure of the membrane domain (Efremov and Sazanov, 2011).
claims.evidence: This is supported by the cited reference.

claims.claim: The peripheral arm structure was solved at 2.1 Å resolution.
claims.source: Here, we present a single-particle cryo-EM structure of the entire E. coli complex I reconstituted into lipid nanodiscs, with the peripheral arm structure solved at 2.1 Å resolution and that of the membrane domain at 3.7 Å.
claims.evidence: This is a primary finding supported by the experimental data.

claims.claim: The membrane domain structure was solved at 3.7 Å resolution.
claims.source: Here, we present a single-particle cryo-EM structure of the entire E. coli complex I reconstituted into lipid nanodiscs, with the peripheral arm structure solved at 2.1 Å resolution and that of the membrane domain at 3.7 Å.
claims.evidence: This is a primary finding supported by the experimental data.

claims.claim: Twin-strep tag was added to genomically encoded subunit NuoF using a CRISPR-Cas9 based system.
claims.source: Twin-strep tag was added to genomically encoded subunit NuoF using a CRISPR-Cas9 based system (Jiang et al., 2015; Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This is a methodological detail supported by the cited reference and figure.

claims.claim: The tagging enabled single-step purification of solubilized complex.
claims.source: This enabled single-step purification of solubilized complex (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A), which was further reconstituted into lipid nanodiscs comprising E. coli polar lipids and membrane scaffold protein MSP2N2 (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A,B).
claims.evidence: This is supported by the experimental data shown in the referenced figure.

claims.claim: The complex was reconstituted into lipid nanodiscs comprising E. coli polar lipids and membrane scaffold protein MSP2N2.
claims.source: This enabled single-step purification of solubilized complex (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A), which was further reconstituted into lipid nanodiscs comprising E. coli polar lipids and membrane scaffold protein MSP2N2 (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A,B).
claims.evidence: This is a methodological detail supported by the experimental data.

claims.claim: Mass photometry indicated that reconstituted complex I was homogeneous and monodisperse.
claims.source: Mass photometry indicated that reconstituted complex I was homogeneous and monodisperse (Figure 1—figure supplement 2C).
claims.evidence: This is supported by the mass photometry data shown in the referenced figure.

claims.claim: Reconstituted complex I was active in catalyzing NADH:ubiquinone-1 (Q1) and NADH:decylubiquinone (DQ) redox reactions.
claims.source: Reconstituted complex I was active in catalyzing NADH:ubiquinone-1 (Q1) and NADH:decylubiquinone (DQ) redox reactions (Figure 1—figure supplement 2D,E).
claims.evidence: This is supported by the activity assay data shown in the referenced figure.

claims.claim: Both NADH:Q1 and NADH:DQ activities were sensitive to Q-site-specific inhibitor piericidin-A.
claims.source: Both NADH:Q1 and NADH:DQ activities were sensitive to Q-site-specific inhibitor piericidin-A but were lower than those of the detergent-purified protein supplemented with lipids (Sazanov et al., 2003) likely reflecting reduced solubility of hydrophobic electron acceptors in the absence or at low concentration of detergent.
claims.evidence: This is supported by the activity assay data.

claims.claim: NADH:Q1 and NADH:DQ activities were lower than those of the detergent-purified protein supplemented with lipids, likely reflecting reduced solubility of hydrophobic electron acceptors.
claims.source: Both NADH:Q1 and NADH:DQ activities were sensitive to Q-site-specific inhibitor piericidin-A but were lower than those of the detergent-purified protein supplemented with lipids (Sazanov et al., 2003) likely reflecting reduced solubility of hydrophobic electron acceptors in the absence or at low concentration of detergent.
claims.evidence: This is an interpretation of the activity data, comparing to cited reference.

claims.claim: The lipid environment provided by the nanodisc is expected to mimic closely lipid vesicles in which reconstituted purified E. coli complex I was shown to pump protons.
claims.source: While without compartmentalization the proton translocation activity cannot be assessed, the lipid environment provided by the nanodisc is expected to mimic closely lipid vesicles in which reconstituted purified E. coli complex I was shown to pump protons (Steimle et al., 2011).
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the cited reference showing proton pumping in vesicles.

claims.claim: Multiple conformations of the complex that differed by relative positions of the peripheral and membrane arms were revealed by 3D classification.
claims.source: Multiple conformations of the complex that differed by relative positions of the peripheral and membrane arms were revealed by 3D classification (Figure 1—figure supplements 4 and 5).
claims.evidence: This is supported by the cryo-EM data processing results shown in the referenced figures.

claims.claim: Three conformations of the entire complex were reconstructed to average resolutions between 3.3 and 3.7 Å.
claims.source: Three conformations of the entire complex were reconstructed to average resolutions between 3.3 and 3.7 Å (Figure 1—figure supplement 4) resolving the interface between the arms; however, due to high-residual mobility of the arms, the antiporter-like subunits were resolved at below 8 Å (Figure 1—figure supplement 4).
claims.evidence: This is supported by the cryo-EM reconstruction data shown in the referenced figure.

claims.claim: Due to high-residual mobility of the arms, the antiporter-like subunits were resolved at below 8 Å.
claims.source: Three conformations of the entire complex were reconstructed to average resolutions between 3.3 and 3.7 Å (Figure 1—figure supplement 4) resolving the interface between the arms; however, due to high-residual mobility of the arms, the antiporter-like subunits were resolved at below 8 Å (Figure 1—figure supplement 4).
claims.evidence: This is an interpretation of the cryo-EM data explaining the resolution limitations.

claims.claim: Focused refinement of each arm separately and subtraction of nanodisc density improved the resolution of peripheral and membrane arms to 2.7 Å and 3.9 Å, respectively.
claims.source: Focused refinement of each arm separately and subtraction of nanodisc density (Figure 1—figure supplement 3) improved the resolution of peripheral and membrane arms to 2.7 Å and 3.9 Å, respectively (Figure 1—figure supplements 3 and 4, Table 1).
claims.evidence: This is supported by the data processing results shown in the referenced figures and table.

claims.claim: After density modification, the resolution of membrane arm improved to 3.7 Å.
claims.source: After density modification (Terwilliger et al., 2020), the resolution of membrane arm improved to 3.7 Å.
claims.evidence: This is supported by the data processing results using the cited method.

claims.claim: Large fraction of the particles corresponds to the peripheral arm only, which may have dissociated during cryo-EM sample preparation.
claims.source: Micrograph analysis, in contrast to mass photometry, revealed that large fraction of the particles corresponds to the peripheral arm only (Figure 1—figure supplement 3) that may have dissociated during cryo-EM sample preparation.
claims.evidence: This is an observation from the cryo-EM data with an inference about the cause.

claims.claim: Dissociated peripheral arm particles yielded 3D reconstruction to 2.8 Å resolution.
claims.source: These yielded 3D reconstruction to 2.8 Å resolution (Figure 1—figure supplement 3), similar to the map of the peripheral arm of intact complex I.
claims.evidence: This is supported by the cryo-EM reconstruction data.

claims.claim: Joining two subsets and applying density modification improved resolution of the peripheral arm to 2.1 Å.
claims.source: Joining two subsets and applying density modification improved resolution of the peripheral arm to 2.1 Å (Table 1, Figure 1—figure supplements 4 and 6).
claims.evidence: This is supported by the data processing results shown in the referenced table and figures.

claims.claim: The final models include 4618 residues that account for 94.7% of the total polypeptide constituting the complex.
claims.source: The final models include 4618 residues that account for 94.7% of the total polypeptide constituting the complex (Table 2).
claims.evidence: This is supported by the model building results shown in the referenced table.

claims.claim: The fold and arrangement of the E. coli complex I subunits is mainly similar to the structures of other complex I homologs.
claims.source: The fold and arrangement of the E. coli complex I subunits is mainly similar to the structures of other complex I homologs.
claims.evidence: This is based on structural comparison with other complex I structures.

claims.claim: High RMSD values for structural alignments reflect long-range twisting and bending of arms observed between complex I from different species.
claims.source: Somewhat high values of RMSD obtained for structural alignments of the entire complexes or its individual arms to Thermus thermophilus [RMSD 7.3 Å (4199 Cα) for entire complex, 4.3 Å (2070 Cα) for membrane arm, and 8.1 Å (2129 Cα) for peripheral arm] and ovine enzyme [8.5 Å (4007 Cα) for entire complex, 5.0 Å (1969 Cα) for membrane arm, and 8.4 Å (2038 Cα) for the peripheral arm] (Figure 1B) reflect long-range twisting and bending of arms observed between complex I from different species (Agip et al., 2018; Baradaran et al., 2013; Vinothkumar et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: This is an interpretation of the structural alignment data, supported by cited references.

claims.claim: E. coli complex I conformations revealed two modes of relative arm rotation.
claims.source: Comparison of E. coli complex I conformations reconstructed to better than 4 Å resolution revealed two modes of relative arm rotation (Figure 1C): (1) rotation around an axis that passes through the NuoH-NuoB interface and is tilted around 45 degrees out of the plane formed by the arms with an amplitude of at least 13 degrees, and (2) rotation around an axis parallel to the membrane and roughly perpendicular to the long axis of the membrane arm with an amplitude of approximately 4 degrees.
claims.evidence: This is based on analysis of the different conformations resolved by cryo-EM.

claims.claim: Relative arm movements in E. coli complex I have larger amplitudes and more diverse directionality than in mammalian and T. thermophilus complex I.
claims.source: Although relative arm movements were observed in mammalian (Kampjut and Sazanov, 2020; Zhu et al., 2016) and T. thermophilus complex I (Gutiérrez-Fernández et al., 2020), their amplitudes were smaller and movement directionality was less diverse.
claims.evidence: This is a comparison with cited references showing differences in conformational dynamics.

claims.claim: Despite significant relative arm movements, the structure of each arm was rigid and did not reveal different conformations apart from specific local dynamics.
claims.source: Despite significant relative arm movements, the structure of each arm was rigid and did not reveal different conformations apart from the specific local dynamics discussed below.
claims.evidence: This is an observation from the structural analysis.

claims.claim: At 2.1 Å resolution, conformations of most side chains in the peripheral arm, positions of ions, and multiple water molecules were resolved unambiguously.
claims.source: At an average resolution of 2.1 Å with the local resolution in the core reaching 2.0 Å (Figure 1—figure supplement 4) conformations of most side chains in the peripheral arm, positions of ions, and multiple water molecules were resolved unambiguously (Figure 2, Figure 1—figure supplement 6).
claims.evidence: This is supported by the high-resolution cryo-EM map.

claims.claim: E. coli subunits NuoC and NuoD are joined in a single polypeptide, unlike other structurally characterized homologues.
claims.source: Unlike other structurally characterized homologues, E. coli subunits NuoC and NuoD are joined in a single polypeptide.
claims.evidence: This is a structural observation unique to E. coli complex I.

claims.claim: The 35 amino acid-long linker between NuoC and NuoD includes an α-helix (residues 180–194) that interacts with subunit NuoB.
claims.source: The 35 amino acid-long linker includes an α-helix (residues 180–194) that interacts with subunit NuoB (Figure 2A).
claims.evidence: This is supported by the structural data shown in the referenced figure.

claims.claim: The relative positions of all redox centers with FMN and nine iron-sulfur clusters, including off path cluster N7, are particularly well conserved.
claims.source: The relative positions of all redox centers with FMN and nine iron-sulfur clusters, including off path cluster N7 (Sazanov and Hinchliffe, 2006), are particularly well conserved (Figure 2C).
claims.evidence: This is based on structural comparison with other complex I structures and the cited reference.

claims.claim: E. coli peripheral arm has ordered C-terminal extensions in subunits NuoB, NuoI, and NuoF with lengths of 22–45 residues.
claims.source: A distinctive feature of the E. coli peripheral arm is the presence of ordered C-terminal extensions in subunits NuoB, NuoI, and NuoF with a length of 22–45 residues and a large 94 residue insertion loop in subunit NuoG, referred to as the G-loop (Figure 2A, Table 3).
claims.evidence: This is supported by the structural data shown in the referenced figure and table.

claims.claim: E. coli peripheral arm has a large 94 residue insertion loop in subunit NuoG, referred to as the G-loop.
claims.source: A distinctive feature of the E. coli peripheral arm is the presence of ordered C-terminal extensions in subunits NuoB, NuoI, and NuoF with a length of 22–45 residues and a large 94 residue insertion loop in subunit NuoG, referred to as the G-loop (Figure 2A, Table 3).
claims.evidence: This is supported by the structural data shown in the referenced figure and table.

claims.claim: These extensions are unique among structurally characterized complex I homologues and have a well-defined structure.
claims.source: These extensions are unique among structurally characterized complex I homologues and have a well-defined structure.
claims.evidence: This is based on comparison with other complex I structures.

claims.claim: The extensions increase the interaction surface between the electron acceptor module and connecting module by a factor of three (from 1400 to 4600 Å2).
claims.source: Similarly, the G-loop fills a crevice between NuoCD, NuoI, and NuoG subunits (Figure 2A) and together with the extensions increase the interaction surface between the electron acceptor module (NuoEFG) and connecting module (NuoICDB) by a factor of three (from 1400 to 4600 Å2), thus stabilizing the peripheral arm assembly.
claims.evidence: This is based on structural analysis of the interface areas.

claims.claim: The structural features (extensions and G-loop) are conserved within the Enterobacteriaceae family and are very common in the phylum Gammaproteobacteria.
claims.source: These structural features are conserved within the Enterobacteriaceae family, are very common in the phylum Gammaproteobacteria and display high conservation of interfacial residues, particularly for the G-loop (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This is based on sequence conservation analysis shown in the referenced figure.

claims.claim: The extensions demonstrate a new evolutionary strategy for complex stabilization that was not observed in other complex I homologs.
claims.source: They demonstrate a new evolutionary strategy for complex stabilization that was not observed in other complex I homologs.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the structural observations and comparison with other homologs.

claims.claim: A strong density near the NuoG surface coordinated by GAsp617, GGln632, GGlu647, GAsp731 and four water molecules was assigned to a Ca2+ ion.
claims.source: A strong density near the NuoG surface coordinated by GAsp617, GGln632, GGlu647, GAsp731 and four water molecules (Figure 2B) was assigned to a Ca2+ ion.
claims.evidence: This is based on the structural data and coordination geometry shown in the referenced figure.

claims.claim: The coordination number, geometry, and ion-ligand distances of ca 2.5 Å support the assignment to Ca2+.
claims.source: The coordination number, geometry, and ion-ligand distances of ca 2.5 Å (Zheng et al., 2008) as well as the 2 mM concentration of Ca2+ in the buffer support this assignment.
claims.evidence: This is based on structural analysis and the cited reference on coordination chemistry.

claims.claim: Divalent ions are known to increase both the activity and stability of E. coli complex I.
claims.source: Divalent ions are known to increase both the activity and stability of E. coli complex I (Sazanov et al., 2003).
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge supported by the cited reference.

claims.claim: GAsp731, one of the calcium ligands, is part of the G-loop, suggesting that Ca2+ stabilizes the fold of the G-loop and consequently, the peripheral arm.
claims.source: One of the calcium ligands, GAsp731, is part of the G-loop, suggesting that Ca2+ stabilizes the fold of the G-loop and consequently, the peripheral arm.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the structural observation of Ca2+ coordination.

claims.claim: The extensions spatially overlap with the supernumerary subunits of complex I from T. thermophilus and the structurally conserved supernumerary subunits of eukaryotic complex I.
claims.source: The extensions spatially overlap with the supernumerary subunits of complex I from T. thermophilus (Sazanov and Hinchliffe, 2006) and the structurally conserved supernumerary subunits of eukaryotic complex I (Zhu et al., 2016; Table 3), consistent with the suggestion that the primary role of supernumerary subunits is to stabilize the complex (Fiedorczuk et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: This is based on structural comparison and supports the cited hypothesis about supernumerary subunit function.

claims.claim: 1170 water molecules associated with the peripheral arm were modeled at 2.1 Å resolution.
claims.source: At 2.1 Å resolution, 1170 water molecules associated with the peripheral arm were modeled (Figure 2D).
claims.evidence: This is supported by the high-resolution structural data.

claims.claim: The positions of 180 water molecules are conserved with those identified in the peripheral arm of ovine complex I.
claims.source: The positions of 180 water molecules are conserved with those identified in the peripheral arm of ovine complex I (Kampjut and Sazanov, 2020; Figure 2D, red spheres).
claims.evidence: This is based on comparison with the cited structure.

claims.claim: Most conserved waters are buried in the interior of the subunits, shielded from the solvent, and likely play a structural role in stabilizing the subunit fold.
claims.source: Most of conserved waters are buried in the interior of the subunits, shielded from the solvent, and likely play a structural role in stabilizing the subunit fold.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the structural positions of the water molecules.

claims.claim: Only a few waters interact closely with iron-sulfur clusters and may influence their potential.
claims.source: Only a few waters interact closely with iron-sulfur clusters and may influence their potential (Tables 4 and 5).
claims.evidence: This is based on structural analysis shown in the referenced tables.

claims.claim: Water molecules close to or between iron-sulfur clusters are not more conserved than those in other parts of the complex, suggesting they were not evolutionary selected to optimize electron transfer rate.
claims.source: The water molecules close to or between iron-sulfur clusters are not more conserved than those in the other parts of the complex, suggesting that they were not evolutionary selected to optimize the rate of electron transfer as was suggested (Schulte et al., 2019).
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on conservation analysis that contradicts a cited hypothesis.

claims.claim: The FMN conformation and key water molecules in the NADH-binding pocket are conserved.
claims.source: The FMN conformation and key water molecules in the NADH-binding pocket are conserved (Kampjut and Sazanov, 2020; Schulte et al., 2019).
claims.evidence: This is based on comparison with cited structures.

claims.claim: Water molecule W1060 is hydrogen bonded to the isoalloxazine ring N5 atom of FMN and to FGlu92, which likely acts as the activating group during catalysis of hydride transfer from NADH.
claims.source: This includes W1060, hydrogen bonded to the isoalloxazine ring N5 atom of FMN and to FGlu92, which likely acts as the activating group during catalysis of hydride transfer from NADH (Fraaije et al., 2000; Figure 3A).
claims.evidence: This is based on structural observation and the cited reference on catalytic mechanism.

claims.claim: The structure does not support the involvement of FGlu93 carbonyl oxygen flipping in ROS regulation as previously suggested.
claims.source: Schulte et.al. (Schulte et al., 2019) suggested a mechanism for regulation of reactive oxygen species (ROS) generation by E. coli complex I that involves flipping the carbonyl oxygen of FGlu93 upon enzymatic reduction. Our structure unambiguously places the corresponding carbonyl oxygen in a conformation that points away from FMN (Figure 3A) similar to conformations found in the reduced and oxidized ovine complex I (Kampjut and Sazanov, 2020), which does not support its involvement in ROS regulation.
claims.evidence: This is based on structural observation that contradicts a cited hypothesis.

claims.claim: E. coli-specific FHis400 replaces Leu residues found in other homologues and is in Van der Waals contact with the isoalloxazine ring of FMN.
claims.source: E. coli-specific features in the FMN-binding pocket include FHis400 that replaces the Leu residues found in other homologues. FHis400 is in Van der Waals contact with the isoalloxazine ring of FMN; its imidazole ring interacts directly with the N3 cluster iron atom and forms a hydrogen bond with Sγ of FCys357 coordinating N3 (Figure 3A).
claims.evidence: This is based on structural observation and comparison with other homologs.

claims.claim: FHis400 imidazole ring interacts directly with the N3 cluster iron atom and forms a hydrogen bond with Sγ of FCys357 coordinating N3.
claims.source: E. coli-specific features in the FMN-binding pocket include FHis400 that replaces the Leu residues found in other homologues. FHis400 is in Van der Waals contact with the isoalloxazine ring of FMN; its imidazole ring interacts directly with the N3 cluster iron atom and forms a hydrogen bond with Sγ of FCys357 coordinating N3 (Figure 3A).
claims.evidence: This is based on structural observation shown in the referenced figure.

claims.claim: FHis400 is solvent-accessible even in the presence of NADH, and may become protonated upon N3 reduction.
claims.source: FHis400 is solvent-accessible even in the presence of NADH, and therefore, may become protonated upon N3 reduction.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the structural observation of solvent accessibility.

claims.claim: FArg320 is positioned such that it can form hydrogen bonds with the ribose moiety of the NADH nicotinamide group and may stabilize bound dinucleotide.
claims.source: FArg320 is positioned such that it can form hydrogen bonds with the ribose moiety of the NADH nicotinamide group and may stabilize bound dinucleotide (Figure 3A).
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the structural position shown in the referenced figure.

claims.claim: Both Arg320F and His400F may serve to counter-balance the negative charges of electrons on N1a and N3 clusters and to increase protein stability.
claims.source: Both Arg320F and His400F may serve to counter-balance the negative charges of electrons on N1a and N3 clusters and to increase protein stability.
claims.evidence: This is a speculation based on the structural positions of these residues.

claims.claim: The structure does not reveal specific features explaining the decreased affinity for FMN in the reduced enzyme.
claims.source: The structure does not reveal specific features explaining the decreased affinity for FMN in the reduced enzyme (Holt et al., 2016). This can be attributed to minor conformational changes in the pocket upon enzyme reduction.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the absence of obvious structural differences and the cited reference.

claims.claim: The Q-binding site in complex I is formed at the end of a crevice between NuoD and NuoB subunits.
claims.source: The Q-binding site in complex I is formed at the end of a crevice between NuoD and NuoB subunits (Baradaran et al., 2013).
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge supported by the cited reference.

claims.claim: In E. coli, the Q-binding wedge is formed by the 58–69 stretch of NuoB and the tip of the 220–225 loop from subunit NuoD.
claims.source: In E. coli, this wedge is formed by the 58–69 stretch of NuoB and the tip of the 220–225 loop from subunit NuoD.
claims.evidence: This is based on structural observation.

claims.claim: DTyr273 and DHis224 are conserved in E. coli and point toward the quinone binding site.
claims.source: Both DTyr273 and DHis224, found in the proximity of bound decylubiquinone (Baradaran et al., 2013) are conserved in E. coli and point toward the quinone binding site (Figure 3D), whereas the tip of the 218–223 loop is flexible as in many complex I structures.
claims.evidence: This is based on structural observation and comparison with the cited reference.

claims.claim: The tip of the 218–223 loop is flexible as in many complex I structures.
claims.source: Both DTyr273 and DHis224, found in the proximity of bound decylubiquinone (Baradaran et al., 2013) are conserved in E. coli and point toward the quinone binding site (Figure 3D), whereas the tip of the 218–223 loop is flexible as in many complex I structures.

claims.claim: The mechanism suggests that a pH jump creates a proton motive force between the sealed Q-cavity and periplasmic surface and might be used to trap equilibrium conformations associated with proton translocation by the membrane domain of complex I.

results.result: The authors determined the cryo-EM structure of the entire catalytically active E. coli complex I reconstituted into lipid nanodiscs, achieving 2.1 Å resolution for the peripheral arm and 3.7 Å for the membrane domain. The reconstituted complex was shown to be active in NADH:Q1 and NADH:DQ redox reactions, sensitive to piericidin-A inhibition, and homogeneous by mass photometry.
results.evaluation: Claims C4, C37-C55 collectively describe the successful structural determination of E. coli complex I in nanodiscs with detailed resolution metrics, supported by extensive cryo-EM data processing (C47-C54), activity assays (C43-C45), and quality control measurements (C42). The methodological approach using CRISPR-Cas9 tagging (C39), nanodisc reconstitution (C40-C41), and multi-step refinement procedures is well-documented with referenced figures and tables.

results.result: E. coli complex I displays highly dynamic connections between peripheral and membrane domains, with two distinct modes of relative arm rotation (13° and 4° amplitudes) that are larger and more diverse than in mammalian and T. thermophilus complex I. Despite these movements, each arm remains structurally rigid.
results.evaluation: Claims C5, C56-C60 are supported by cryo-EM data showing multiple conformations (C47, C58) with quantified rotation angles and axes. The comparison with other species (C57, C59) is backed by structural alignments and cited references. The observation of rigid individual arms despite inter-arm flexibility (C60) is consistent with the data processing showing distinct conformations.

results.result: The E. coli peripheral arm is stabilized by unique structural features including C-terminal extensions in NuoB, NuoI, and NuoF (22-45 residues) and a 94-residue G-loop in NuoG. These extensions increase the interaction surface between electron acceptor and connecting modules by threefold (1400 to 4600 Å²) and represent a novel evolutionary strategy for complex stabilization not observed in other homologs.
results.evaluation: Claims C6, C62-C70, C145-C147 are well-supported by high-resolution structural data (C61) showing well-defined structures for these extensions. The quantification of interface areas (C68), conservation analysis within Gammaproteobacteria (C69), and comparison with supernumerary subunits in other species (C75) provide strong evidence. The evolutionary interpretation (C70, C147) is a reasonable inference from the structural observations.

results.result: A Ca²⁺ ion was identified near the NuoG surface, coordinated by four acidic residues and four water molecules with ion-ligand distances of ~2.5 Å. One ligand (GAsp731) is part of the G-loop, suggesting Ca²⁺ stabilizes the G-loop fold and consequently the peripheral arm.
results.evaluation: Claims C71-C74 are supported by structural data showing appropriate coordination geometry (C72) and consistency with known Ca²⁺ effects on complex I stability (C73). The assignment is reasonable given the coordination environment, buffer composition, and cited reference on metal coordination chemistry. The inference about G-loop stabilization (C74) is logical given the structural position.

results.result: At 2.1 Å resolution, 1170 water molecules were modeled in the peripheral arm, with 180 positions conserved with ovine complex I. Most conserved waters are buried and likely play structural roles, while waters near iron-sulfur clusters show no greater conservation than elsewhere, contradicting the hypothesis that they were selected to optimize electron transfer rates.
results.evaluation: Claims C76-C80 are supported by the high-resolution structure enabling water molecule identification. The conservation analysis (C77) is based on comparison with cited structures. The inference about structural roles (C78) is reasonable for buried waters. The conclusion about electron transfer optimization (C80) appropriately challenges a prior hypothesis with conservation data, though this is a negative result requiring careful interpretation.

results.result: The FMN-binding pocket shows conserved features including key water molecules and FGlu92 positioning for catalysis. E. coli-specific features include FHis400 (replacing Leu) that contacts FMN and N3 cluster, and FArg320 positioned to stabilize NADH. The structure does not support a previously proposed ROS regulation mechanism involving FGlu93 carbonyl flipping.
results.evaluation: Claims C81-C89 are supported by high-resolution structural data (C61) showing unambiguous side chain conformations. The comparison with other species (C81, C84) and contradiction of a prior hypothesis (C83) are based on clear structural evidence. The speculative elements (C86-C88) are appropriately qualified as possibilities. The inability to explain FMN affinity changes (C89) is honestly acknowledged.

results.result: The Q-binding site is formed between NuoD and NuoB subunits, with conserved residues DTyr273 and DHis224 pointing toward the quinone binding site. The tip of the D218-223 loop is flexible as in other complex I structures.
results.evaluation: Claims C90-C93 are supported by structural data and comparison with cited references (C90, C92). The observations about conserved residues (C92) and loop flexibility (C93) are consistent with other complex I structures, providing validation.

results.result: At 2.1 Å resolution, iron-sulfur cluster atoms are resolved as independent density blobs with unambiguous side chain conformations. Three E. coli-specific structural differences explain the uniquely high potential (~-0.3 V) of cluster N1a: EAsn142 hydrogen bonding to ECys97, water molecule W74 in a cavity created by EGly140, and backbone nitrogen of FGly97 hydrogen bonding to ECys133.
results.evaluation: Claims C94-C103 are strongly supported by high-resolution structural data enabling detailed analysis of cluster environments. The explanation for N1a potential (C97-C100) is supported by structural comparison with other species and consistency with mutagenesis data (C98). The structural basis is clearly defined with specific residues and distances.

results.result: The N2 cluster shows lower potential in E. coli (-220 mV) compared to mammalian complex I (-140 mV), despite very conserved polar environment. Dimethylation of 49kDaArg85 in mammalian enzyme prevents hydrogen bonding with BCys63, which should decrease N2 potential. Computational modeling will be required to explain the potential differences.
results.evaluation: Claims C104-C108 present a paradox: E. coli N2 has lower potential despite the mammalian enzyme having a modification (C107) that should decrease potential. The structural conservation (C105) contradicts the observed potential difference (C104). The call for computational modeling (C108) acknowledges this cannot be resolved with current structural data alone. This represents an unresolved question rather than a supported conclusion.

results.result: The complete membrane arm structure including NuoH was determined at 3.5-4.0 Å resolution in lipid nanodiscs. The nanodisc density is clearly visible as a ~30 Å thick belt matching the hydrophobic surface. The structure is very similar to the detergent-solubilized crystal structure (RMSD 1.1 Å), confirming the membrane curvature is not an artifact. However, the N-terminus of NuoH (residues 1-52, including HTMH1) is completely missing.
results.evaluation: Claims C109-C116 are supported by cryo-EM data showing clear nanodisc density (C110-C112) and structural comparison with prior crystal structure (C113). The missing HTMH1 density (C116) is a clear observation from the reconstructions. The inference that membrane curvature is not an artifact (C114) is reasonable given the similarity between structures in different environments.

results.result: The structure visualizes a complete chain of charged residues connecting the Q-site with antiporter-like subunits. However, analysis indicates no continuous proton path exists between the Q-site and NuoN in E. coli. The conserved HLys274 is positioned off the main proposed translocation pathways.
results.evaluation: Claims C117-C119 are supported by structural analysis of cavities and residue positions. The conclusion about lack of continuous proton path (C118) is based on distance measurements and cavity analysis, though this is an inference from static structure. The observation about HLys274 (C119) is qualified by noting side chain flexibility could allow alternative positions.

results.result: The cytoplasmic half of JTMH3 is well-resolved, suggesting absence of alternative conformations seen in eukaryotic complex I. In contrast, MTMH8 shows poor, fragmented density between residues 255-265, indicating multiple conformations. This localized disorder near the π-bulge may indicate involvement in proton translocation.
results.evaluation: Claims C120-C124 are supported by density quality analysis. The absence of JTMH3 conformational heterogeneity (C120) contrasts with cited eukaryotic structures. The MTMH8 disorder (C121-C122) is clearly observed in the density. The speculation about functional significance (C124) is appropriately qualified as a possibility based on the structural position.

results.result: The interface between peripheral and membrane arms shows unusual features in E. coli complex I. NuoB and NuoD are rotated ~15° relative to other species, causing >10 Å shift of the NuoD interfacial region and separation from NuoH. The conserved ATMH1-TMH2 loop fragment is disordered. This creates openings large enough for water/proton exchange between Q-cavity and bulk solvent, suggesting an uncoupled state where redox reactions are not coupled to proton translocation.
results.evaluation: Claims C125-C135 are supported by structural comparison showing quantified rotations (C131) and shifts (C132). The observation of disordered loop (C133) and interface openings (C134) is based on structural analysis. The interpretation as an uncoupled state (C135) is a reasonable inference from the disrupted interface, though this represents a static snapshot and the functional state remains to be confirmed experimentally.

results.result: The detergent-solubilized complex is catalytically active and was solved to 6.7 Å resolution. It also displays high arm mobility and uncoupled conformation, with the peripheral arm rotated even further from the expected coupled position than in nanodiscs. HTMH1 is resolved but weakly and bent. Comparison of sample preparation conditions indicates neither air-water interface nor nanodisc reconstitution causes the uncoupled conformations.
results.evaluation: Claims C136-C143 are supported by activity assays (C136), cryo-EM data (C137-C139), and structural comparison. The observation of HTMH1 in detergent but not nanodiscs (C141-C142) is clearly documented. The conclusion about sample preparation artifacts (C140) is a reasonable inference from comparing the two conditions, though the true cause of uncoupling remains uncertain.

results.result: E. coli complex I, with the smallest number of subunits among structurally characterized homologs, evolved unique stabilization strategies (extensions, G-loop, Ca²⁺). The membrane arm reveals no continuous proton path to NuoN and no JTMH3 conformational states seen in mammalian complex I. MTMH8 shows localized disorder, representing the first indication of conformational changes in antiporter-like subunits. The high flexibility between rigid arms explains the known fragility of E. coli complex I.
results.evaluation: Claims C144-C157 synthesize multiple structural observations into an integrated understanding of E. coli complex I features. The conclusions about stabilization strategies (C145-C147), lack of continuous proton path (C148), and conformational dynamics (C149-C152) are supported by the structural data. The explanation for known flexibility (C153-C154) is consistent with the observed conformational heterogeneity. The interpretation as uncoupled state (C156) is reasonable but the cause remains unclear (C157).

results.result: The reasons for the uncoupled conformation are unclear. It may result from lipid bilayer mimetics not sufficiently resembling native bilayer, or may represent a functional resting state analogous to the deactive state in eukaryotic complex I. The absence of HTMH1 density in nanodiscs but not detergent is unique to E. coli, but comparison indicates this is neither the cause of uncoupling nor high arm mobility.
results.evaluation: Claims C158-C163 acknowledge significant uncertainty about the functional significance of the observed conformation. The two proposed explanations (C158-C159) are speculative and cannot be distinguished with current data. The comparison with eukaryotic deactive state (C160) shows differences that weaken the analogy. The conclusion about HTMH1 (C163) is based on comparison but doesn't resolve the underlying question of whether the structure represents a physiological state.

results.result: The authors propose a new hypothetical coupling mechanism where coupling is enabled by forming a sealed Q-cavity accessible only to neutral electron acceptors. Ubiquinone reduction decreases proton activity in the cavity, which is rectified by proton transfer through NuoH from the periplasm, coupled to transfer of three protons through antiporter-like subunits in the opposite direction (net 2H⁺/e⁻). The membrane module functions as a 1H⁺in/3H⁺out antiporter operating by alternating access mechanism.
results.evaluation: Claims C165-C173 present a speculative mechanistic model that is not directly supported by the structural data. The model is inconsistent with the observed uncoupled conformation showing an open Q-cavity (C134, C155). While the model is constrained by structural observations (C167), it requires the sealed cavity that is not observed in the structures. The mechanism is presented as hypothetical (C165) but lacks experimental validation. This represents a theoretical proposal requiring future testing rather than a supported result from the current work.

results.result: The introduction establishes the biological context and prior knowledge about complex I structure and function, including its role in electron transfer and proton translocation, conserved architecture across species, and the gap in structural knowledge for E. coli complex I despite extensive functional characterization.
results.evaluation: Claims C1-C36 represent established knowledge and accurate characterization of the field, supported by appropriate citations. These provide necessary context for the study but are not novel findings. The assessment that E. coli complex I structure was unknown (C3, C36) and that proposed mechanisms remain speculative (C32) accurately represents the state of knowledge prior to this work.
